subject: Geografi
title: Natural resources and energy
sourceSummary: What separates renewable from non-renewable resources, where in the world the most important resources are found, the pros and cons of different energy sources, how fresh water is distributed, and why resource use is so uneven between rich and poor countries.
topics: where resources are found in the world
pros and cons of energy sources
resource use in rich and poor countries

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a non-renewable natural resource?
questions.opener: A non-renewable resource is not replenished within human timescales – once it has been extracted, it is gone.
choices: Wind power
Solar energy
Oil
Forest
questions.explanation: Oil has formed over millions of years from the remains of plants and animals, so once it is pumped up and burned it cannot be replaced – it is non-renewable. Wind and sun are constantly renewed, and forest counts as renewable as long as planting and felling are kept in balance.

questions.topic: where resources are found in the world
questions.prompt: In which part of the world are some of the largest known oil reserves found?
questions.opener: Countries such as Saudi Arabia, Iraq and Kuwait are located there.
choices: Northern Europe
The area around the Persian Gulf in the Middle East
Central Africa
Southeast Asia
questions.explanation: The countries around the Persian Gulf – including Saudi Arabia, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates – hold a very large share of the world's known oil reserves, which has given them great economic and political importance. The North Sea has oil but in significantly smaller quantities, and Central Africa and Southeast Asia have other important resources, such as minerals and tropical timber.

questions.topic: pros and cons of energy sources
questions.prompt: What is a disadvantage of hydropower?
questions.opener: Think about what happens to the river and the landscape when a dam is built.
choices: It releases a lot of carbon dioxide when the electricity is produced
It provides very little electricity relative to the cost
The fuel runs out quickly
Dams change the river's ecosystem and can force people to move
questions.explanation: Hydropower produces large amounts of electricity with almost no emissions, but building dams holds back rivers, blocks fish migration, changes the ecosystem, and can put villages and farmland under water. Carbon dioxide emissions from power production and fuel running out are instead problems associated with fossil fuels.

questions.topic: pros and cons of energy sources
questions.prompt: Which energy sources account for the largest share of Sweden's electricity production?
questions.opener: Think about the rivers in Norrland and the large power stations on the coast.
choices: Hydropower and nuclear power, together with rapidly growing wind power
Coal power and oil-fired power stations
Solar power and biogas
Natural gas and peat
questions.explanation: Sweden's electricity comes mainly from hydropower and nuclear power, while wind power has grown strongly in recent years – together they give an electricity production with low carbon dioxide emissions. Coal, oil and natural gas are used very sparingly in Swedish electricity production, unlike in many other countries.

questions.prompt: How large a share of the Earth's water is fresh water that people can easily use?
questions.opener: Most of the water on Earth is in the oceans, and a large part of the fresh water is frozen.
choices: About half
About a quarter
A very small share – most is salt water or locked up in glaciers and deep ground
Almost all of it, but it is unevenly distributed
questions.explanation: Around 97 per cent of the Earth's water is salt water, and of the small amount of fresh water that exists, most is locked up in glaciers, ice sheets and deep groundwater – only a fraction of a per cent is easily accessible in lakes and rivers. That is why water scarcity is a growing problem in many regions despite the Earth looking water-rich.

questions.topic: resource use in rich and poor countries
questions.prompt: What does an ecological footprint measure?
questions.opener: The measure converts our consumption into how much nature it requires.
choices: How much waste a household throws away per week
How much nature and natural resources a person or a country consumes
How large an area a country covers on the map
How many degrees the temperature rises in a country
questions.explanation: The ecological footprint converts food, transport, housing and goods into the area of nature required to produce them and absorb the emissions – often expressed as a "number of Earths" if everyone lived the same way. The amount of waste is only a small part of this, and a country's area on the map has nothing to do with the measure.

questions.topic: resource use in rich and poor countries
questions.prompt: Explain why a person in a high-income country consumes significantly more natural resources than a person in a low-income country.
questions.opener: Go through an ordinary day: how you travel, what you eat, how you live and what you buy.
questions.answer: The difference is down to consumption level and lifestyle. In a high-income country, people travel further and more often by car and plane, live in larger, heated homes with many appliances, eat more meat and dairy products that require a lot of land, water and feed, and often buy new clothes and electronics that are replaced at a fast pace. Each such item requires metals, energy and transport, and much of the production also takes place in other countries – the emissions and resource extraction happen there, but the item is used here. In a low-income country, income is much lower, food is more often plant-based and locally produced, travel is shorter and possessions are fewer and used for longer. That is why the ecological footprint per person can differ many times over between countries.
steps: Higher income means people can buy more goods, energy and travel.
Transport: cars and planes require large amounts of fossil energy compared with walking, cycling and buses.
Housing: larger homes that are heated or cooled, plus many electrical appliances.
Food: a lot of meat and dairy requires more land, feed and water than a plant-based diet.
Goods: clothes, electronics and furniture are often replaced, and the resources are also often extracted in other countries than where the item is used.

questions.prompt: Summarise natural resources, energy sources and water.
questions.opener: Think resource types, where they are found, the pros and cons of energy sources, and how water is distributed.
questions.answer: Natural resource: something in nature that humans use · renewable: sun, wind, water, waves, geothermal energy, forest and fish (if used at the rate they are replenished) · non-renewable: oil, coal, natural gas, uranium and metals formed over millions of years · fossil fuels cause carbon dioxide emissions and climate impact but are easy to store and transport · nuclear power: low carbon dioxide emissions and a lot of electricity, but radioactive waste and high construction costs · hydropower: a lot of electricity and controllable, but dams damage ecosystems and can force people to move · wind power and solar power: no emissions during operation but vary with the weather and require materials for the installations · bioenergy: renewable if the forest regrows, but competes for land · Sweden's electricity comes mainly from hydropower, nuclear power and wind power · resources are unevenly distributed: oil around the Persian Gulf, iron in Australia, Brazil and Sweden, copper in Chile, rare earth metals in China · water: about 97 per cent is salt water and much of the fresh water is locked up in ice, so only a fraction is easy to use · water scarcity and falling groundwater levels are big problems in dry areas · ecological footprint: a measure of how much nature a person or a country consumes – many times greater in high-income countries than in low-income countries.

questions.topic: pros and cons of energy sources
questions.prompt: What is an advantage of solar energy compared with fossil fuels?
questions.opener: Think about what comes out of the chimney at a coal power plant compared with a solar panel.
choices: It works just as well at night as during the day
It requires no materials at all to manufacture
It always produces more electricity overall than hydropower
It produces no greenhouse gas emissions when the electricity is generated
questions.explanation: Solar panels produce electricity with no greenhouse gas emissions during operation, unlike fossil fuels, which release carbon dioxide when burned. Solar energy does, however, require materials to manufacture the panels, produces no electricity at night, and today accounts for a smaller share of the world's electricity overall than hydropower.

questions.topic: where resources are found in the world
questions.prompt: In which country are some of the world's largest iron ore deposits found, including at the mining town of Kiruna?
questions.opener: This country is in northern Europe and has a long tradition of mining.
choices: Japan
The Netherlands
Denmark
Sweden
questions.explanation: Sweden, with among other things the large mines in Kiruna and Malmberget, is one of the world's most important producers of iron ore. Japan, the Netherlands and Denmark, on the other hand, lack significant iron ore deposits of that scale.

questions.prompt: Does fish count as a renewable or a non-renewable resource?
questions.opener: Think about whether fish stocks can recover, and what determines that.
choices: Always non-renewable, no matter how much fishing takes place
Neither renewable nor non-renewable
Renewable only in fresh water, never in the sea
Renewable, if fishing happens at the rate stocks can recover
questions.explanation: Fish is a renewable resource because stocks can reproduce and recover, but only if fishing doesn't happen faster than they can reproduce – overfishing can otherwise cause stocks to collapse almost like a non-renewable resource. This applies both in fresh water and at sea, not just one or the other.

questions.opener: Think about where rainwater goes after it has sunk down through the soil layers.
choices: Another word for seawater
Rain that hasn't yet reached the ground
Water that is only stored in glaciers
Water stored below the ground surface in soil and bedrock
questions.explanation: Groundwater is water that has seeped down through the soil layers and collected in pores and cracks below the ground surface, and it's an important source of drinking water in many parts of the world. It is therefore neither seawater, rain in the air, nor only ice in glaciers.

questions.topic: resource use in rich and poor countries
questions.prompt: What does it mean if a country's ecological footprint corresponds to "three Earths"?
questions.opener: Think about what the measure actually converts to.
choices: That the country's area is three times bigger than planned
That the country produces food for three times more people than it has inhabitants
That the country has too few inhabitants for its area
That three Earths would be needed if everyone lived and consumed like the average inhabitant of that country
questions.explanation: An ecological footprint of "three Earths" means that if the whole world's population consumed as much nature and resources as the average inhabitant of that country, three Earths would be needed for it to be sustainable in the long run. It is therefore about consumption in relation to the Earth's carrying capacity, not about the country's own area or food production.

questions.topic: pros and cons of energy sources
questions.prompt: What is a disadvantage of nuclear power?
questions.opener: Think about what's left over after the fuel has been used.
choices: It causes large carbon dioxide emissions during operation
It can only be used in countries near the equator
It depends on wind to function
It produces radioactive waste that must be stored safely for a very long time
questions.explanation: Nuclear power does produce low carbon dioxide emissions during operation, but it creates radioactive waste that must be handled and stored safely for tens of thousands of years, and it also requires very high investment costs. It depends neither on wind nor is it limited to countries near the equator.

questions.topic: where resources are found in the world
questions.prompt: Where in the world is a large share of the rare earth metals used in mobile phones and computers mined?
questions.opener: This country is also the world's most populous industrial nation and a major producer of electronics.
choices: Iceland
New Zealand
Portugal
China
questions.explanation: China accounts for a very large share of the world's extraction and processing of rare earth metals, which are used in everything from mobile phones to wind turbines. Iceland, New Zealand and Portugal, on the other hand, play no significant role in that production.
